title: Half-year update: Q1–Q2 2026
content:
_Note: We wrote most of this update about a month ago, focusing on the first half of the year. We’ve recently been putting out a lot of new content in response to the fast-changing public sentiment around Hugging Face and existential risk — you can find some of that content on our landing page [here](https://80000hours.org/hugging-face/), including [our most popular video monologue to date](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xOi5nDH0lu0)._

## **Major updates**

**We’re growing our capacity to support our ambition**

We think 80,000 Hours can deliver significantly more than it does today, so a big theme of the last (and next!) year has been growing our capacity to match those ambitions. Around 20 new staff joined in the first half of 2026, with hires across almost every team, and we’re setting up an in-house recruiting team to keep hiring at pace.

Some examples of what we’re doing (and plan to do) with this capacity include: releasing much more content, getting it from production to release faster, and experimenting with new formats; scaling headhunting and better tailoring it to what hiring managers need; and creating room to explore new products or programmes that seem especially promising.

We’re also making some changes to our senior leadership team and working to make our culture even more fast-moving and innovative. Michelle Hutchinson is now director of strategy and studio, Brenton Mayer has moved to director of special projects, and Sashika Coxhead has taken over as director of operations. Unfortunately, Arden Koehler, our long-time director of web, decided to move on from 80,000 Hours. Until we confirm a long-term director of web, Bella Forristal has taken over as interim director in addition to her role as director of growth.

**Our latest product — the AI Advisor — is live**

We’ve launched our [AI Advisor](https://app.80000hours.org/) which has been in beta since last year — meaning we can now offer personalised guidance to far more people than our advisors can speak with directly. The AI Advisor gives users personalised, research-based advice on career decisions, recommends job openings matched to their background, keeps track of their applications, lets them work through exercises from the career guide, and more. We’ve put a lot of work into the quality, including checks to make sure it doesn’t give users an unduly positive evaluation of their fit for roles. So far, 738 users have rated it an average of 6.1 out of 7.

**Our updated**[**career guide**](https://80000hours.org/book)**was released by Penguin and is now in bookstores**

Our goal in republishing was to reach new users via launch publicity, prestige, and translations. We managed to achieve international bestseller status, hitting #3 on _The Sunday Times_ list and making the _USA Today_ list, but unfortunately missing out on _The New York Times_ bestseller list. It’s now the most complete single introduction to our career advice, with new chapters on why AI is the most pressing issue facing society and how it will affect the job market. Up to the end of July, we’d sold ~15,000 copies, which is slightly above our modal prediction.

**We’re investing in our Substack**

We’re using [our Substack](https://80000hours.substack.com/) to reach the growing audience following the career advice and AI conversation there, and to host timelier writing than the evergreen advice on our website. It features guest posts from writers like [Lawrence Chan](https://80000hours.substack.com/p/openais-rogue-ai-agents-hacked-a) alongside our own content, including profiles like this one on [how to get into AI safety](https://80000hours.substack.com/p/how-three-mid-career-professionals), effective career advice like [how to become a better applicant](https://80000hours.substack.com/p/high-impact-roles-hire-differently), and topical pieces like the one on [Ted Chiang and AI consciousness](https://80000hours.substack.com/p/ted-chiang-is-wildly-overconfident). We’re approaching 7,000 subscribers after six months, with 76% subscriber and 447% view count growth in Q3, mostly through discovery within Substack’s ecosystem.

## **Programmes and hiring updates**

**Studio (formerly Podcast)**

*   We’ve renamed the podcast team to the studio team, reflecting our intention of putting out a large quantity and variety of content over the coming years.
*   Tom Reed and Zershaaneh Qureshi joined as hosts, Nick Stockton and Elizabeth Cox joined as producers, Dominic Armstrong joined as production coordinator, and Lou Moran joined as studio associate.
*   We’ve been experimenting with new formats: Rob’s monologues have been performing well (with his recent ‘[What the hell happened with AGI timelines in 2026?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=31Uhv12ZLHU)‘ video becoming one of our most popular episodes to date, with over 150,000 views on YouTube), and Zershaaneh is testing debate-style content in Q3.

**Video**

*   We released two new videos on our [AI in Context](https://www.youtube.com/@AI_In_Context) YouTube channel: one on the book [_If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nl7-bRFSZBs), and one on the [OpenAI board drama](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_eYTkvZqbnQ).
*   Our [MechaHitler video](https://80000hours.org/videos/mechahitler/) won the Webby People’s Voice Award for [Best Documentary Storytelling](https://winners.webbyawards.com/2026/video-film/performance-craft/best-documentary-storytelling/374292/if-you-remember-one-ai-disaster-make-it-this-one).
*   Each of our four long-form videos has now passed two million views(!), with the AI in Context channel itself passing 400,000 subscribers and 20 million total views.
*   We’ve been experimenting working with external scriptwriters. We’re also exploring a new channel with its own host, aimed at a younger audience.

**Web**

*   Arden Koehler, who has led the web team for the last 5.5 years, has decided to move on from 80,000 Hours. Bella Forristal has taken over as interim director of web in addition to her role as director of growth.
*   We’ve started prioritising content that targets people already concerned about AI and are looking for ways to help, leaving first exposure to higher-reach channels like AI in Context.
*   We redesigned our [career reviews page](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/) to make it easier to navigate, and published eight new reviews, including [AI policy in the US government](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-policy-us-government/), [AI security](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-security/), and [technical governance](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/technical-governance/). We also published the [updated career guide](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/) on our site alongside the book launch.
*   We hired a new writer-researcher, a content associate, and product manager, and we’re hiring an additional writer-researcher.

**Marketing and growth**

*   Our growth function has entered an exploration phase, systematically investigating new growth opportunities for 80,000 Hours — though we expect further progress here to be delayed while Bella runs the web team.
*   In Q2, we also led on the launch of our [career guide](https://80000hours.org/book/) with Penguin.
*   Some internal analysis has made us more confident in marketing’s impact, and in response we’ve ramped up marketing spend after deciding to reduce investment in Q2 2025.
*   Coefficient Giving funded our marketing budget for the next year, and we’re hiring to support the scaleup.

**Advising**

*   After a couple of advisors moved on, we ran a hiring push in Q2. We’re aiming to grow from two to six advisors, and have so far made two new hires: Carrick Flynn and Emily Dardaman. We also hired Louise Verkin as a programme specialist to maintain and improve the systems advising runs on.
*   We delivered around 500 calls in the first half of the year, and hope that hiring will increase this rate — due to our low capacity we’ve unfortunately had to defer some applicants who met our normal bar, asking them to reapply in a couple of months.

**Headhunting**

*   The headhunting team runs candidate searches for high-priority roles using a database of ~17,000 candidates, and combines LLM-driven evaluation with human review. The level of human review is calibrated to the impact of the role: searches range from fully automated to human curated.
*   So far, we’ve learnt of 19 counterfactual placements in 2025 — cases where our search resulted in someone taking a role the hiring organisation likely wouldn’t have otherwise identified.
*   We’re aiming to significantly increase this team’s output because we currently only run searches for around half the roles we think matter most, and because the hires that do happen through headhunting look particularly unlikely to have happened otherwise.
*   We brought on Brian Tan as a headhunting product specialist to oversee search delivery, and we’re now hiring for multiple roles: a talent database lead, 1–3 headhunting specialists/associates to deliver searches, and an additional product specialist.

**Job board**

*   In July, we brought the [job board](https://jobs.80000hours.org/?jb_source=2026__10__half-year-update-q1-q2-2026) more in line with our focus on making advanced AI go well: we no longer post higher-experience roles in global health, animal welfare, and climate change, though we’ve kept early-career roles in those areas since we think much of their value comes from career capital. You can read more about the reasoning behind the change in this [blog post](https://80000hours.org/2026/07/why-were-increasing-the-ai-focus-of-our-job-board/).
*   We now list [courses](https://jobs.80000hours.org/?refinementList%5Btags_role_type%5D%5B0%5D=Course&jb_source=2026__10__half-year-update-q1-q2-2026) on the main job board, which help people with promising skill sets build context in areas like AI safety.
*   So far in 2026, we’ve learnt of 28 full-time placements; 31 part-time, fellowship, internship, or funding placements; and 57 course and programme placements. Compared to what we knew at this point last year, this indicates a drop in full-time placements, and growth in fellowships and course placements.

**AI products**

*   The [AI Advisor](https://app.80000hours.org/) (covered in the major updates above) is the work of our AI products team, which has grown from an experimental one-person effort into an established three-person subteam within career services.

**Operations**

*   Sashika Coxhead, previously head of people, became director of operations in June. Brenton Mayer, who has led our operations team since 2019, moved into a new role as director of special projects, focusing full time on high priority projects across the org.
*   Inés Fernandez stepped into a new role as recruiting lead.
*   We launched a multi-role hiring round across our business operations, people operations, and recruiting teams. So far, we’ve:
    *   Hired Sam Pickering and Sara Recktenwald to the business operations team.
    *   Hired Anna Lopez to the recruiting team.

*   We closed our 2025 financial accounts and completed 80,000 Hours’s first audit as an independent organisation.

## Content highlights

A few standouts from our recent content:

*   An updated comprehensive introduction to [_How AI could create the world’s biggest problems_](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/artificial-intelligence/) (problem profile)
*   [_You really should, unfortunately, be worried about Sam Altman_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_eYTkvZqbnQ) (AI in Context video)
*   [_Ajeya Cotra on whether it’s crazy that every AI company’s safety plan is ‘use AI to make AI safe’_](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ajeya-cotra-transformative-ai-crunch-time/) (podcast episode)

You can find all our content releases [here](https://80000hours.org/topics/#list-of-everything).

title: Things people don’t say
content:
Marketers and politicians too.

We don’t say them because it’s assumed. And because we’re afraid.

“I might be wrong.”

“I’m just guessing”

“This might be selfishly motivated.”

“It could be that I’m hallucinating.”

“I heard this somewhere but I don’t know firsthand that it’s true.”

“I know I sound certain, but I’m not.”

When an AI doesn’t say these things, we’re frustrated when they turn out to be the case. Because our default in interactions with machines is that they don’t dissemble, confuse or mislead.

Perhaps we should print these caveats out and read them before we read an ad, believe a scammy text or interact with an LLM.

Trust is the building block of cultures that matter. We have long manipulated trust for commercial and political ends, and now machines are following our lead.

title: Our Messy Cyborg Past and Future
content:
A few decades ago, cultural historian and author Mike Jay stumbled onto the unfortunate story of James Tilly Matthews. In 1797, Matthews was locked in a London psychiatric hospital known colloquially as Bedlam because he had become convinced that his mind was being controlled by a machine he called the “air loom.” That machine, he believed, manipulated his mind via a magnet that had been secretly planted in his brain by political operatives.

This was a florid fantasy, but Jay was fascinated by the echoes Matthews’ delusion contained of many real-life, cutting-edge technologies in development in the 1980s, two centuries later. As Jay attempted to trace the history of ideas about brain-technology hybrids back to their points of origin, he realized that such cyborgian notions had persisted throughout the industrial age. They were embedded in science fiction but also repeatedly brought to life in scientific invention, though the quest was always incomplete.

**Read more: “**[**We’ve Got News for You About Supercharging Your Brain**](https://nautil.us/weve-got-news-for-you-about-supercharging-your-brain-243328)**”**

“The imagined locus of the magnetic or electronic brain device is always in the future, where it will control our minds or endow us with superhuman powers, attack us with invisible rays or create seamless virtual realities,” Jay writes in the introduction to his new book, _Wireheads_: _An Unnatural History of Technology in the Brain_ which tracks the course of this history.

I spoke with Jay about the ways culture and science can become mismatched when it comes to cyborgian fantasies, whether all brain-machine hybrids are technologies of transcendence, a device called the “God helmet,” his dislike of AI, and the dominant voices of technofuturism.

**You write in the book that you first encountered the term “wireheads” in Bruce Sterling’s science fiction novel****_Schismatrix_, where it was used as a contemptuous term to describe people who lived off grid. That’s sort of a fun twist because you would think wireheads would connote the opposite. Was there something about this double meaning that you felt made it especially fitting as the title for the book?**

Where I first came across the term “wirehead” was in _Schismatrix_, but it predates that. It started to be used in the 1970s. The idea was that people were going to get addicted to sticking electricity into the pleasure centers of their brains, which was a thing back then when people believed that brains had pleasure centers and you could stimulate yourself with them.

It became a term for the ultimate addiction to technology. I liked it as a term because it suggests that there’s a slightly retro history of the future. I’m trying to give the idea that this isn’t the first time we’ve conceived of these things that we’re used to talking about rather breathlessly as in the future.

There’s actually a history to this kind of speculation. I’ve heard people use the term wireheads to mean electronics geeks and people who are very into technology. It’s one of those words that rings bells, but nobody quite knows what it means. That’s a bit of an invitation for a writer to kind of fix it and appropriate it.

**You write in the introduction that the book is about these disputed borderlands where science and fiction are impossible to separate. Where are some of those borderlands today?**

If I was writing this book 30 or 40 years ago, there’d be an enormous number of news stories to pull out of the air—from all the _Clockwork Orange_ stuff about whether you can suppress violent impulses to, “Is there a godspot and can we give ourselves religious experiences?” All these are a little in the rearview mirror now.

Whenever I mention what I’m writing about now, everybody straight away goes, “Oh, Neuralink,” that’s kind of our one cultural reference these days, and I think it’s telling that there’s only one. But I think that’s a good example. I mean, when we talk about that, are we talking about what Neuralink is actually doing, which is producing extremely sophisticated medical technologies for probably quite a small number of people with very severe physical disabilities?

Or are we talking about Elon Musk’s sales pitch for Neuralink, which is, “We’re all gonna have these chips in our brains, and we’re all gonna be super intelligent, and our consciousness is gonna be uploaded to AI or the cloud or maybe on Mars or whatever.”

You still have today a mixture of ideas which, if you follow them back, actually come from the 1980s and 1990s and cyberpunk fiction, but they overlaid on the technology of today. That’s a recursive process that’s been happening for a long time.

**How so?**

There are a lot of stories in this book that have that arc when you trace them through. The one about having a pleasure center in the brain that we can stimulate is a good example. It starts off with a piece of science, with some work that suggests this, and then that goes viral into the culture, and you get lots of futurologists and science fiction writers riffing on it. And then it all becomes familiar to us from _Barbarella_ and the orgasmatron or other cultural tropes.

It’s only after this process has happened—that it’s gone from science into the wider culture—that two or three decades later, scientists circle back and go, “Oh, actually there isn’t a pleasure center in the brain. That was an idea we had before the neurotransmitter revolution, and now we know that we have different neurotransmitters and different circuits and pathways in the brain. And it’s all much more complicated than we thought.”

You often get this thing where culture leaps on an early scientific discovery, and then afterwards, the science turns out not to be what we thought it was, but of course it’s still out there in the culture.

**The scientists and the wider culture do seem often to become misaligned. You describe a few researchers who are very surprised by this gap. José Delgado and Robert Heath, for example, thought the mind control devices they were experimenting with would liberate humanity. They were not expecting hostile reactions to their work from people in the general public who saw more authoritarian implications. I thought that was such an interesting tension between what the researchers intended and how the public interpreted it.**

Yes, they were all fascinating characters. José Delgado and James Olds and Robert Heath were some of the very earliest people to introduce electrodes and two-way signaling into animals’ brains, rats or bulls. They were operating in that white heat of early brain science, which was all unfolding against, on the one hand, the Cold War, and then on the other hand, the beginnings of the counterculture.

And a lot of people involved in cybernetics made that transition. They started off working within Cold War science and ended up in the ‘60s becoming part of the holistic consciousness revolution. You can see how those figures at that time started off with a belief in their liberal mission of science to save the world and restore and guard reason against the forces of unreason and propaganda.

But then they were blindsided when people looked at this from the outside and went, “You’re going to do what? You’re going to stick electrodes into people’s brains and control their behavior?” They’ve got themselves into a position where they believed this was a liberal thing to do because it would give power back to reason and civilization and take it away from our violent impulses and things that science has now made it possible for us to control.

**Can you tell the story of the God helmet?**

Yes, I followed this story quite carefully. This was a Canadian psychiatrist called Michael Persinger, who had been working with EEG and patients with epilepsy. And he had EEG readings on a patient who had a temporal lobe seizure, and she came back with this very quiet conviction, “I just saw God. He was right here. I was just with him.”And Persinger had the EEG reading that corresponded to this religious experience stored. So he developed a helmet, being Canadian, of course, it was a snowmobile helmet with electromagnetic coils in the headpieces. And it sent a very, very weak current pattern with this signal across the temporal lobes. And he started administering this to people in a darkened room, and people started having religious experiences when it was turned on. I remember some early reports.

I remember a big one in _Wired_ magazine. People would traipse up there and put the God helmet on and have these religious experiences. I was fascinated. I was invited to try the God helmet on, but it was in Paris and expenses weren’t paid, so I didn’t quite get that. This was in the middle of the rise of neurotheology and the Decade of the Brain. People were asking, “Is there a godspot?” This religious experience in the brain became a sort of focus for a lot of that debate.

As it became a focus for that debate, people started paying a bit more attention. Other people tried to replicate Persinger’s findings and couldn’t. And then he gave his equipment to a Swedish lab who did the same thing, but with a double-blind methodology, so nobody knew, operators or subjects, whether the machine was switched on or off. And what they discovered was that people in the God helmets did have strange mystical experiences or a sensed presence or a belief that something was out there, something from outside their minds had entered. But people had these experiences also when the machine was switched off, so it’s that placebo effect again.

It was interesting for me going back to that 10 years later, because I knew a few people who had been involved in parapsychology research and had said at the time, “Oh my God, this is amazing. You gotta try it.” And I circled back to them 10 years later, and they were like, “Oh, yeah, I’m not sure if that really works. Oh yeah, I think I’ve got one in the attic still, but I haven’t dug it up for years.” So it became a vanished story. It felt like a contemporary story, but it’s kind of history now.

**You write that the God helmet fits in a long line of technologies of transcendence. Are all of our brain machines, in some sense, technologies of transcendence?**

I think they can be, and I think that’s one of the meanings they’ve always had. But they’re also technologies of control, which I guess is the opposite, in the same way that they’re technologies of medicine and healing, but they’re also technologies of paranoia and mind control.

I’m trying to communicate these contradictions in the way I’ve structured the book. Rather than structure it around this or that kind of device, I’ve structured it around our aspirations and our hopes and our fears and our ideas of what these things might do.

The idea that they might be technologies of transcendence goes way back. Someone like William Crookes, who was president of the Royal Society in Britain, and who was also very active in the Society for Psychical Research, gave a great lecture to an audience of electrical engineers saying, “You know, maybe there’s an organ in the brain that we don’t know about that picks up electrical frequencies that we can’t perceive in any other way.”

We still have these conversations. How exactly do migrating animals know where magnetic north is? Is there some kind of sixth sense there? But 150 years ago, people were talking about this. Maybe we can find a device and a signal that activates this part of the brain and maybe that’s gonna make it possible for us to connect with the spirit world or maybe this is how telepathy works. Maybe there are these signals that are moving between our brains in ways that we can’t notice. That’s one of the ideas that’s attached to technology in the brain from right from the beginning.

**You quote William Gibson as saying, “The future is already here. It’s just not very evenly distributed.” Gibson’s idea is that the present contains the seeds of the future, but also the remnants of the “derelict utopias” of the past, whose original intentions have become warped. With each new generation, it seems we become convinced that technology will bring some kind of utopia, only to find that it makes the powerful more powerful and the vulnerable more vulnerable. Why don’t we learn that lesson?**

I think because it does both things at the same time. Certainly, if you think of the internet revolution, all the rhetoric around that early on was about how “Information wants to be free,” that it was giving power to individuals, which it was. But at the same time, it was giving enormous information-gathering powers of control to governments and corporations.

I was never a big fan of golden age sci-fi because it was always these gleaming futuristic worlds where everything was new and perfect. That was one of the things that always appealed to me about William Gibson. The remains of the old world persist, and projects that hadn’t turned out as their architects had wanted had been co-opted in ways that were different from what their originators thought they were going to be. The future, like the present, is always going to be messy.

**You describe one of the first novels to feature a machine-enhanced brain, called****_The Clockwork Man_****, set in the year 8000, and published in 1923 by London playwright and magazine editor E.V. Odle. In the future of the novel, humans have internalized their machines, which opens up all kinds of technological miracles but also meshes humanity more tightly “to the cogs of the machine.” These clockwork humans, as you describe them, have lost some of their humanity and cannot function without their clocks, which seems very apt for today. Can humans devise machines that don’t deprive them of their humanity?**

There’s a nice line of Marshall McLuhan’s that I quote where he says, “We always become robots when we’re uncritically engaged with our technologies.” And that sticks with me. I’m very aware that when you’re tapping away on your phone or your laptop, when you’re just clicking this and tapping that, you’re actually the robot, you know?

You give an agency over to the device. I guess that’s an individual decision. I think for a lot of people it’s coming up with AI and the attempts to market AI as the solution for all our problems. I haven’t engaged with AI and I think a lot of people haven’t, and the backlash against it suggests that we’re all a little concerned about becoming robots if we give all our mental processes creative iterations over to the machine.

**You write that predictions, in addition to being great metaphors, can be agents of propaganda by directing our attention, directing investment. I recently spoke with science fiction writer Daniel H. Wilson, who is best known for writing****_Robopocalypse_****, and he said he had shifted his focus away from dystopias to more hopeful stories in which humans had actually solved some of the problems of the present. Do we need new kinds of hopeful science fiction with new predictions about the future?**

Yeah, I think that’s right. The big tech guys are writing their versions of utopias. That’s what they’re trying to present to us. But I think it’s extraordinary the way in which all our technological futures have become fixated around AI at the moment. There’s not really any other story.

I mean, there are other non-technology stories like climate catastrophe, for example. But I think we have got into a place where it’s very hard to conceive of positive futures, which also ignores a lot of what’s happening now. This book started for me about 30 years ago, and that was just at that moment before the internet and then the smartphone and everything got going.

We have had a technological transformation and it has been extraordinary, you know? The thing about prediction is interesting because people do use prediction to say, “Okay, of all the things going on in the present, this is the important one. This is the one you have to pay attention to. This is the one that’s gonna define the future.” We don't always have to believe that when people say it, but at the same time, the way we’re talking now, for the first half of my life and more, it would have been impossible.

The video phone was one of these things that was always on the horizon and it never happened and it kept being predicted. And then suddenly, there was Skype and then there was FaceTime and now it’s every day. We tend to also underestimate or forget about the extraordinary transformations that technology brings because they become so mundane so fast.

**Have you ever been tempted to write science fiction yourself?**

I did write a little bit when I started out. I wrote screenplays mostly because I was coming out of working in TV, but I decided early on I wasn’t that great at it. I never quite believed my characters, I could never hear them speaking in my head. But the bit I really enjoyed was world building and constructing scenarios. And I discovered that you can do that out of real life and out of history, so I shifted over to non-fiction.

**You mention in the book that the dominant voices of technofuturism have become more explicitly reactionary and anti-feminist, whereas female science fiction authors like Octavia Butler and Ursula K. Le Guin didn’t pay much mind to brain gadgets, compared with their male counterparts. Why do you think that is?**

I think technology has been developed by a very self-selecting elite cadre who are disproportionately young and male and have been very focused on their devices from very early on, and probably less attentive than the rest of us to whatever else is going on in the world: relationships or society or our environment. There’s a Silicon Valley groupthink, which is very streamlined and pushes forward very fast and efficiently towards the future that it envisages. But it’s a two-dimensional future, and its appeal across the broader spectrum of humanity is limited.

**Octavia Butler said in a lecture at MIT that science fiction generally falls into one of three buckets: “what if,” “if only,” or “if this goes on.” And I wondered if you were to speculate, what would you say the science fiction of “if this goes on” would look like?**

It depends what you think of as “this.” When people are put on the spot, most of the present-day trends that they perceive are ones that are going downwards or getting worse. “What if” is the purest form of science fiction speculation, one that’s not attached to any particular vision or any particular future. We get an awful lot more of, “if this goes on.”

You see that, for example, in climate fiction, which has a narrow emotional bandwidth. There’s not a huge variation in tone. There’s an enormous variation in the way that people are constructing ecological futures, but it’s pretty hard for “if this goes on,” to go anywhere other than towards some kind of extended catastrophe. Whereas “what if” opens up all kinds of different possible futures. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Was Human Language Born Around the Campfire?
content:
We gather around campfires and share stories, keeping the darkness at bay to draw each other into worlds of ghosts and monsters, to immerse ourselves in the past and future. Communing around a fire entwines humanity in a yarn stretching back to our hominin ancestors, who stoked these embers of storytelling. And those nightly fires could have been the hearths from which early language emerged.

Hominins began taming fire around 1.5 million years ago, and by 400,000 years ago hearths were more common as our ancestors used fire to chase away darkness at night. The glowing little world that a fire creates around itself, painting cave walls and the faces of our companions in warm hues and lively shadows, calls us in to lean closely and listen. This environment may have ignited a shift from our ancestors communicating about the world around them, to narrating things they could not see. Communication moved from something like the [gestures great apes use today](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/mila.12500), like chest-beating or baring their teeth, toward a simple proto-language that was a step toward modern language, according to an anthropologist and a primatologist who [published](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspb/article/293/2078/20260602/483174/Firelight-and-the-origins-of-spoken) their theory last month.

**Read more: “**[**Human Ancestors Were Using Fire Earlier Than Previously Thought**](https://nautil.us/human-ancestors-were-using-fire-earlier-than-previously-thought-1281795)**”**

“Storytelling really is core to human evolution,” said [Robin Dunbar](https://www.psy.ox.ac.uk/people/robin-dunbar), an emeritus professor of evolutionary psychology at the University of Oxford, who was not involved in the new study but who studies the behavioral, cognitive, and neuroendocrinological mechanisms that underpin social bonding in primates and early humans.

While we can’t know for sure what tales were told around crackling fires hundreds of thousands of years ago, modern day hunter-gatherer communities can illuminate what those ancient nights may have looked like. Anthropologist [Pauline Wiessner](https://search.asu.edu/profile/3034285) worked for decades in Namibia and Botswana among Ju/’hoansi communities, whose nighttime conversations differ dramatically from daytime exchanges. Everyday information and gossip are shared during daylight, but at night, people spin yarns about time travel, humans turning into animals, the moon and the stars, and ghosts and demons.

So what is it about fire that makes us want to tell stories?

The dim luminance of firelight might have something to do with it. Since it’s difficult to see in the low light, shifting to spoken words over gestures has advantages. Low light can also loosen inhibitions around communication, while enhancing storytelling effect. “Body language is dimmed by firelight and awareness of self and others is reduced,” [wrote Wiessner,](https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.1404212111) who did not collaborate on the new research, in a 2014 paper about the Ju/’hoansi. “Facial expressions—flickering with the flames—are either softened, or in the case of fear or anguish, accentuated.”

The [new paper](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspb/article/293/2078/20260602/483174/Firelight-and-the-origins-of-spoken), written by University of Saint Andrews primatologist Catherine Hobaiter and Dartmouth University anthropologist Nathaniel Dominy, takes these concepts a step further, interpreting the fireside as a social niche unique to prehistoric humans and a cradle of human language—an “integrated sensory experience” that intermingled light, color, and rhythm.

Almost completely at the red end of the spectrum, firelight has nearly no blue wavelengths. This type of light partially suppresses melatonin, staving off sleep, but as it dies down, firelight “falls squarely in the optimal range for sleep preparation… with glowing embers providing the best light of all,” Hobaiter and Dominy wrote. This would have extended waking hours without diminishing sleep quality, resulting in a psychological wind down at the end of the day as the fire smouldered.

Firelight also dispenses a large dose of infrared wavelengths. Research suggests true infrared light provides [metabolic benefits](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/11/5134), stimulating energy production in our cells, and helping our bodies process nutrients more efficiently. Around a fire, that might help humans digest food more effectively, or offset the metabolic costs of complicated cognitive processing, said Hobaiter. This dovetails with [an existing theory](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0067270X.2012.756754) suggesting human brains evolved to grow larger, making advanced cognition possible, partly because cooking food over fire unlocked more calories.

Fire’s rhythmic flickering also creates a hypnotic, mesmerizing effect shared among those huddled in its glow. Shared rhythmic activity, such as making music or dancing together, synchronizes our brain waves and [fosters social connection](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0027272). Flickering light can also cause [photic driving](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s002210100682): Our neurons fire in synchrony with the flux of the flame. Around a single communal flickering light, the shared sense of rhythm could synchronize our minds.

“Part of what might instill this deep sense of social connection and social bonding that happens around a fire could be that fire is a point of shared focal, social symmetry—much in the way that when we’re dancing to music together we’ve got a beat,” said Hobaiter. “We’re quite literally ending up on the same wavelength.”

This environment would have been ideal for speaking rather than gesturing, the authors argue, priming humans to use spoken language to communicate beyond immediate experiences, and soar into unseen possibilities, times, and worlds. “You can start to go from ‘what did we do today’ and ‘what will we do tomorrow,’ to ‘what did we do this time last year,’ ‘where do we need to go in a few weeks’ time,’ to then starting to think about these bigger picture, more abstract concepts,” said Hobaiter. This progression would have likely been incremental, she added, baby steps from gestures toward something like pantomime to express more abstract ideas, and eventually from simple vocalizations to more articulated words.

Other theories place the origin of language much later than the origins of taming fire, explained [Ian Tattersall](https://www.amnh.org/research/staff-directory/ian-tattersall), Curator Emeritus of Human Origins at the American Museum of Natural History who studies the evolution of human cognition, and who wasn’t involved in Hobaiter’s and Dominy’s research. For language to emerge, early humans would have needed brains capable of symbolic thought, an anatomical development step that [he suggests happened around 200,000 years ago](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00677/full). Tattersall noted that the earliest evidence of symbolic thought occurred at the [advent of art and artifacts](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12064-010-0093-9) that symbolically represented things in the environment, around 100,000 years ago. He said he sees language as an ability that evolved alongside that cognitive leap.

“Language is a radically different kind of thing from anything that preceded it, and it had to do not only with communication, but with how hominins perceived the world,” Tattersall said.

According to Tattersall, the first control of fire between 1.5 million and 400,000 years ago would have been too early for hominins to have the biological brain capability, and the proven ability in the archaeological record, of symbolic thought necessary to develop language.

Fire is important to human social evolution, and storytelling does go hand in hand with sitting around a fire, Tattersall said, but he claimed that language needed to have existed already before fireside stories could be told—not that taming fire and taming language necessarily emerged in tandem. “I don’t think language was around far back enough to have been a major influence on early sitting around campfires,” Tattersall added. “But I think that once language was available, it completely changed the experience of sitting around a fire.”

Wiessner doesn’t characterize fireside storytelling as the sole catalyst for human language either, as Hobaiter and Dominy propose, but concedes it may have been crucial. Firelight represented an important niche that shaped language evolution and other uniquely human social attributes, according to Wiessner.

By firelight, community members not only share information and strengthen social bonds, continuedWiessner, but they also sense what others are thinking and feeling through stories. Exposure to the range of others’ perspectives and feelings can foster theory of mind and empathy.

“I think the pull [of fire] on language would have been huge here,” said Wiessner. “Having people come together at night, and having these hours of time to interact, probably made a big difference. A really strong force pulling language.”

While the idea that fire facilitated storytelling and language evolution isn’t completely new, said Dunbar, the new paper explores physiological sensitivities to firelight, and the synchrony it may engender, in interesting ways. Like with laughter or dance, [synchrony is extremely important](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/eth.12528) to us as a species. “[In storytelling] you have the audience all taking part in a synchronized way,” said Dunbar. “It creates this wave of bonding and warmth that goes throughout the whole circle—it’s magic.”

Of course, the advent of artificial light dramatically changed humanity’s nighttime rituals, turning darker hours into economically productive time instead of just story time. “The day then ends with the flip of a switch, without taking the time to revisit, explore, ponder, and repair relationships, or let the issues of the day fade with the embers,” wrote Wiessner.

But even today, humans ensconced in the comforts of modern technology continue to seek out time by the fire.

“Fire is at the heart of so many of our social rituals,” said Hobaiter, from gathering near a fireplace in winter to sitting around a bonfire in summer. “This combination of the properties of light, of the social niche that this creates, and of the firelight itself synchronizing our brain activity or behavior with each other, is what’s mediating this sense of social connection.”

The way we fall into a reverie beside a fire lives deep in our bodies, despite layers of modernity. The rhythm of a good story harmonizes with the rhythm of a flickering fire, synchronizing with our brains, integral like our heartbeats. We stay up just a bit later conjuring up what came before us, and what will come after us. A torch passed down over hundreds of thousands of years, our human story blazes in the heart of the communal fire. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

[JC](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

Nature has blessed us with brains that are hardwired to find patterns and recognize faces, so it’s no surprise we tend to notice faces even where there aren’t any. Although they may be better educated, the humans at NASA are no different than the rest of us. They recently [posted](https://x.com/NASA/status/2109320622882873464) an image of a smiley face discovered amongst the stars.

The galaxy cluster SDSS J1038+4849 as imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope._Credit: NASA/ESA_

The photo, originally captured by the Hubble Space Telescope in 2015, shows a galaxy cluster known as SDSS J1038+4849 located 4.5 billion light-years from Earth in the Big Dipper constellation. In the photo, the two yellow “eyes” are actually massive galaxies. The face and smile, on the other hand, are caused by a phenomenon predicted by Einstein’s general theory of relativity: gravitational lensing.

**Read more: “**[**A Look Back at Hubble’s Most Breathtaking Images**](https://nautil.us/a-look-back-at-hubbles-most-breathtaking-images-1281059)”

A sufficiently massive celestial object is capable of distorting spacetime around it, so light that would ordinarily travel in a straight line (or be blocked by it) is instead bent around it. Astronomers and astrophysicists use gravitational lensing to determine the mass of galaxies, locate exoplanets, and even in the search for dark matter.

The smiley face photo features a special case of gravitational lensing called an Einstein ring. When the light source, the gravitational lens, and the observer (in this case Hubble) are all aligned, it produces a ring effect. But to those of us on Earth with socially evolved, pattern-seeking brains, it looks like it’s smiling. ![Image 7](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Elephants Engineer Their Ecosystems Even in Death
content:
Elephants are ecosystem engineers. They trample trees, loosen soil with their tusks, and can even create trails and watering holes. According to a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2605332123) in the _Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences_, these massive beasts continue to sculpt the savannas long after their deaths.

To investigate the impact of elephant carcasses on the ecosystems, biologists from the University of California, Santa Barbara spent nearly eight years sampling the soil and plant life from 40 different carcass sites scattered throughout South Africa’s Kruger National Park.

**Read more: “[Is Poaching Causing Elephants to Evolve Without Tusks?](https://nautil.us/is-poaching-causing-elephants-to-evolve-without-tusks-236248)”**

“My intuition was that, since the carcass was only physically present for a relatively short period, its effect would also be rather muted and transient,” study co-author Izak Smit of the South African National Parks said in a [statement](https://news.ucsb.edu/2026/022853/elephants-continue-shape-savanna-even-after-death). “However, a very different picture emerged when the lab results came back.”

The team discovered a cascade of environmental changes that started unfolding soon after death. First, nutrients from the elephant corpses leached into the ground, altering soil chemistry with nitrogen levels spiking dramatically. “At really fresh carcass sites, soil nitrogen concentrations can be up to 3,000 times higher,” study co-author Courtney Reed of UC Santa Barbara explained. “That’s just insane.”

Rather than stimulating growth, these sky-high nitrogen levels made the soil toxic to plants, but not to the microbes living in the dirt. With a colossal influx of nutrients, bacteria rapidly proliferated—but only a few species. According to the team, a handful of fast-growing bacteria likely out-competed the rest, resulting in a dearth of microbial diversity.

After soil nitrogen levels settled down a bit, plants started to grow, but the researchers found they followed the same pattern as the microbes, with just a few species dominating the carcass site (mostly grasses). According to the team, the nutrient hot spot resulted in a biodiversity cold spot, a dynamic that was present throughout the nearly eight-year study period.

Analysis of the plant leaves also revealed they contained more nutrients. “It turns these grasses from watery iceberg lettuce into a juicy romaine,” senior author Deron Burkepile of UC Santa Barbara said. These lush grasses provided food for grazing herbivores for years, and their droppings kept the sites fertilized.

It’s a lot of ecological activity from just 40 elephant carcasses, and per the team, around 600 elephants die in the preserve each year. Of course, tens of thousands of years ago when megafauna were plentiful, this particular ecological cycle would have been more common. Now elephants are among just a few species of massive animals left, and they’re also endangered.

“Given the magnitude, duration, and ecosystem-spanning integration of these impacts, the loss of megacarcasses could represent a fundamental shift in the structure and function of ecosystems across the globe,” the researchers concluded. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Deep-Sea Mining Faces Another Hurdle—Exploding Rocks
content:
Deep-sea mining may still be in its infancy, but scientists and environmentalists are already [raising the alarm](https://nautil.us/the-oceanic-fallout-of-deep-sea-mining-252542) about the risks. Seafloor massive sulfides that form around hydrothermic vents are rich with valuable metals like copper, gold, silver, and zinc. They’re also home to [unique ecosystems and fauna](https://nautil.us/in-search-of-lifes-smoking-gun-3-237427) that can’t be found anywhere else on Earth (and definitely won’t survive an encounter with mining equipment).

Unfortunately, these deep-sea critters may be caught between red hot demand and dwindling terrestrial supplies (data centers in particular need plenty of copper). The International Seabed Authority, an intergovernmental body that regulates seabed mineral development in international waters, has already greenlit sulfide mineral exploration around two deep-sea ridges. The seldom seen life on the ocean floor might seem like an increasingly tempting sacrifice to mineral-hungry developers, but now there’s a new threat: The rocks themselves can explode.

**Read more: [“The Dubious Economics of Deep-Sea Mining”](https://nautil.us/the-dubious-economics-of-deep-sea-mining-309597)**

According to a new _Scientific Reports_[study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70438-0) by U.S. Geological Survey scientists, metal-sulfide rock samples extracted in 2022 from the Escanaba Trough off the coast of Oregon and California spontaneously combusted in the lab, reaching temperatures above 212 degrees Fahrenheit. “The production of heat through exothermic reactions hasn’t been investigated in seafloor massive sulfide deposits but has the potential to cause rapid onset fires on ships,” the researchers wrote.

These exothermic reactions occurred after two of the rocks were pulverized for study in the lab, so the team analyzed their chemical and physical characteristics to find out why. According to the researchers, they were composed of nanocrystalline marcasite (a form of iron sulfide), which isn’t usually a hazard. Crystals generally tend toward forming the most thermodynamically stable shape, but the structure of these were slightly different and less stable. They also found that the metal sulfides produced more heat when they reacted with oxygen.

The findings mean that mining metal sulfides from the ocean might be a bit riskier than mining them here on land (from prehistoric seabed formations that are now above water). Changes in temperature, atmosphere, and pressure could alter their structures, making them more prone to exploding. Additionally, the researchers stress that the metal sulfides in each seabed formation may have different properties, requiring further study before mining can begin.

Deep-sea life may not be able to fight back against mining operations, but the rocks are a different story. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Check Out the Natural Beauty of the Natural Landscape Photography Awards
content:
Planet Earth offers up stunning scenes every day, and nothing captures these moments better than [the winners of the Natural Landscape Photography Awards](https://naturallandscapeawards.com/2026-competition-results-gallery/).

A total of 11,929 photographs were submitted to the competition, from 1,086 photographers in 52 countries. Here are a few of our favorites—a gorgeous mix of sunrises and sunsets, snowstorms and hailstorms and volcanoes of every sort.

Twenty-seven-year-old Abraham Saikley of the U.S. was named Photographer of the Year. He’s spent the past four years living on the road and photographing some of the most dramatic scenery on the planet. This shot, entitled “Shadow Puppets,” is of the Chaltén Massif mountain range on the border of Argentina and Chile. _Credit: Abraham Saikley_

Lukas Furlan of Austria won Photographer of the Year. Among his submissions was this untitled shot of late-fall weather in the Dolomites in northeastern Italy. _Credit: Lukas Furlan_

This image from Photographer of the Year runner-up Dorin Bofan of Romania features cooling lava seen through hail, snapped at the eruption of the Fagradalsfjall volcano in Iceland. _Credit: Dorin Bofan_

The image above, “The Still Woods,” was captured in Shizuoka, Japan, by KoKi Dote, who was awarded third place in the Photographer of the Year category. Dote himself is from Japan, and he says “everything was still, as though time had stopped” when the photo was taken. _Credit: KoKi Dote_

Gabriel Stankiewicz from Poland captured Project Winner honors for his work under the title “The Pine Constant”—years spent photographing pine forests everywhere from the cold of the Arctic to the warmth of the Mediterranean. This photo, “First Settlers,” is of a high-altitude, volcanic landscape dominated by Canary pines in Tenerife, Spain. _Credit: Gabriel Stankiewicz_

The Project Runner-Up was given to Kenny Muir from the U.K., for his “Caledonian Winter” work photographing the Caledonian Forest in the Scottish Highlands. This dramatic image, “Frozen Forest,” was taken as the morning fog was dispersing, with the rising sun catching some of the forest’s snow-laden branches. _Credit: Kenny Muir_

The Natural Landscape Photography Awards also include several specific categories. “A Breath Between Storms” took home the Grand Landscape prize. It was captured by Swiss photographer Xavier Lequarre in South Lípez, Bolivia, from nearly 14,800 feet up the side of a volcano. _Credit: Xavier Lequarre_

The Intimate Landscape winner was “Drifting Petals, Fading Spring” by Japanese photographer Hiroyuki Tsuchiya. “The scene evokes the quiet transition of seasons—a fleeting sense of spring lingering for a moment before dissolving into time,” explained Tsuchiya. _Credit: Hiroyuki Tsuchiya_

Vincenzo Mazza from Italy secured the Abstract Landscapes award for this photograph of the Skeiðarárjökull glacier in Iceland called “Patterns of Time.” In the words of Mazza: “The patterns of volcanic ash, blending seamlessly with the cracks and crevasses of the ice, tell the story of a timeless ballet between fire and ice.” _Credit: Vincenzo Mazza_

Julian Łoziński from Poland won the Multiple Exposure and ICM (Intentional Camera Movement) category for “Layers of Tree and Water.” This image was captured by a lake in southern Sweden as the sun was setting. The six-shot multiple exposure of trees and their reflections was created entirely in camera. _Credit: Julian Łoziński_

The Waterscapes category went to Annette Cuthbertson’s “4’s company, 5’s a crowd.” The location is Assynt, in the Northern Scottish Highlands, and the photo was taken during a break in a storm—a few moments when “the scene came alive,” Cuthbertson says. _Credit: Annette Cuthbertson_

title: Triplet of ‘Ghostly’ Galaxies Hints at What Dark Matter Is — and Isn’t
content:
A collision may have left these galaxies without dark matter. That spells trouble for alternative gravity theories.

![Image 1](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Dark-Matter-Galaxies-cr.several-Lede-scaled.webp)

The lack of dark matter in galaxies DF2, DF9, and DF4 (clockwise from left) was a shock to scientists, who speculate that they formed after an ancient collision.

NASA, ESA, and P. van Dokkum (Yale University); M. A. Keim/HST; Van Dokkum, P., Shen, Z., Keim, M.A. et al

## Introduction

About 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don’t look quite right. They aren’t whirlpools bursting with light, but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” said [Michael Keim (opens a new tab)](https://astronomy.yale.edu/people/michael-keim), an astrophysicist at Yale University. And this isn’t even the weirdest thing about them.

Dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together. It draws ordinary, visible matter toward it, allowing stars to form and keeping the stelliferous limbs of galaxies from flying off. “Almost all galaxies are dominated by dark matter,” said [Shyam Balaji (opens a new tab)](https://www.kcl.ac.uk/people/shyam-balaji), a theoretical physicist at King’s College London.

But these three diffuse galaxies, known as DF2, DF4, and DF9, have left astronomers stunned. After using a suite of telescopes to estimate their masses — using the motions of their stars as a proxy — the researchers found that all three have little dark matter. Instead, a pittance of ordinary matter alone must have forged their small selection of stars. How could these rule-breaking galaxies have formed?

A [paper (opens a new tab)](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/1538-4357/ae6b8d) published in June 2026 in _The Astrophysical Journal_ offers a potential solution. Once upon a time, two regular galaxies collided. Their ordinary matter — their gas and dust — swirled about and got clumped up. But the dark matter passed right through and continued on, like a specter passing through a wall. The cosmic pileup left behind three new galaxies, each bereft of dark matter, each left to struggle to form a new batch of stars.

It’s a convincing explanation for many experts — one that, crucially, may tell us something about the mystery of dark matter.

Some scientists have suggested that dark matter, which has yet to be directly detected, may not exist. Instead, they propose that a tweak to our understanding of the gravitational force might explain various features of the universe.

These bizarre galaxies pour cold water on that idea. “What this is showing is that dark matter is … not just a modification of gravity,” said Keim, who is an author of the new study. If you segregate ordinary matter from dark matter, you’d expect that the dark matter–lacking galaxies would struggle to form stars — and that’s what DF2, DF4, and DF9 show.

That suggests, as many have suspected for some time, that dark matter is a physical thing. “The absence of dark matter is, in a way, some evidence of dark matter, which is ironic,” Balaji said.

## **Dark Ghosts**

What, exactly, is dark matter? Ever since it was formally proposed by the astronomer Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s — and built upon in the 1970s by the astronomer Vera Rubin — cosmologists and astrophysicists have been putting forward their best candidates. Could it be a [stealthy type of neutrino](https://www.quantamagazine.org/experiments-ring-the-death-knell-for-sterile-neutrinos-20260408/)? Might it be so-called weakly interacting massive particles, or [WIMPs](https://www.quantamagazine.org/physicists-are-expanding-the-search-for-dark-matter-20201123/)? Some have even opined that it could be [primordial black holes](https://www.quantamagazine.org/monster-neutrino-could-be-a-messenger-of-ancient-black-holes-20260123/) as small as individual atoms and as old as the universe itself.

“We don’t know which dark matter candidate is the right one,” said [Daniel Whiteson (opens a new tab)](https://sites.uci.edu/daniel/), a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine. Whatever it is, it has yet to be detected. But “there’s a lot of independent lines of evidence that dark matter _is_ matter.”

![Image 2](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/KeckObservatory-crWMKeckObservatory_EthanTweedie.webp)

In 2018, scientists used observations from the Keck Observatory in Hawai‘i to estimate the mass of galaxy DF2. They discovered that it contained 400 times less dark matter than expected.

WM Keck Observatory/Ethan Tweedie

Dark matter, which makes up 27% of the universe — and 85% of all matter —interacts with gravity. If it were down to the gravitational pull of ordinary matter alone, stars on the edges of rapidly spinning galaxies would escape into space. Ordinary matter alone would struggle to clump together tightly enough to form stars. Dark matter also seems to warp space itself, bending light around objects in a process known as gravitational lensing.

“You wouldn’t get galaxies without dark matter,” said [Chamkaur Ghag (opens a new tab)](https://profiles.ucl.ac.uk/35464-chamkaur-ghag), a physicist at University College London. “Is there a way of evolving the galaxies without dark matter in the first place? Our understanding says no.”

So when [DF2 (opens a new tab)](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/dark-matter-goes-missing-in-oddball-galaxy/) was discovered in 2018, astronomers didn’t quite know what to make of it. The galaxy is roughly the same size as the Milky Way, but with 200 times fewer stars, it’s considerably dimmer. Suspicious, scientists used the Keck Observatory in Hawai‘i to track the motions of those stars to estimate its total mass. They discovered that, even for such a star-deficient galaxy, it was lightweight: It seemed to contain, at most, 400 times less dark matter than they would expect, making DF2 the first dark matter–deficient galaxy ever spotted.

In 2019, they observed [DF4 (opens a new tab)](https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/news/dark-matter-deficient-galaxy), another phantom galaxy with a dearth of dark matter. And in 2026, scientists announced that a third, DF9, had joined the club. It contains the mass of roughly 100 million suns, which is consistent with having only ordinary matter. If it were also packed with dark matter, it would be 100 times more massive.

That all three gossamer galaxies existed along a line, as neighbors, didn’t escape the attention of astrophysicists, who began to coalesce [around an origin story (opens a new tab)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04665-6).

![Image 3](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Glaxies-Aligned-cr.ESA_Hubble_NASA_DigitizedSkySurvey2_Acknowledgement_DavidedeMartin.webp)

This image from the Hubble Space Telescope shows neighboring galaxies DF2, DF9, and DF4. An ancient smash-up may have stripped away their dark matter, leaving only ordinary matter behind.

ESA/Hubble/NASA/Digitized Sky Survey 2/Acknowledgement: Davide de Martin

Dark matter is only known to act with the gravitational force; there’s no compelling evidence yet that it interacts with other fundamental forces, like electromagnetism. If two typical galaxies met in a head-on collision, the dark matter would experience very little friction, or drag, and would keep on rocketing by. But ordinary matter, which interacts using all four fundamental forces, would get all tangled up.

“An analogy would be two knights jousting, where the knights and their lances collide and may be thrown to the ground in a heap, while their horses keep on running at full speed,” said [Aaron Romanowsky (opens a new tab)](https://www.sjsu.edu/people/aaron.romanowsky/), an astronomer at San José State University.

## **Trouble for Modified Gravity**

Several independent experts buy the tale spun by Keim and his colleagues. “It’s very convincing,” Whiteson said.

It’s reminiscent of the [Bullet Cluster (opens a new tab)](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/nasa-webb-pierces-bullet-cluster-refines-its-mass/), two massive collections of galaxies 3.8 billion light-years away that also collided eons ago. This destruction derby, which was recently observed by the James Webb Space Telescope, has a messy distribution of mass that only makes sense if dark matter and ordinary matter [got torn asunder (opens a new tab)](https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Images/2007/07/The_Bullet_Cluster2) during the collision.

Although this kind of segregation can be seen with greater clarity in DF2, DF4, and DF9, not everyone agrees on how the separation took place.

[Kinwah Wu (opens a new tab)](https://profiles.ucl.ac.uk/10719-kinwah-wu), a theoretical astrophysicist at University College London, noted that the triplet does not exhibit any of the [fluid, wispy features (opens a new tab)](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/a-collision-in-the-heart-of-a-galaxy/) that one would expect to see after a galactic collision. He suggests that, in this case, DF2, DF4, and DF9 were passing through a large group of massive galaxies. This outsize rabble then stripped the triplet of all their dark matter during their ill-fated voyage.

![Image 4](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Bullet-Cluster-cr.NASA_-scaled.webp)

The Bullet Cluster is the result of a massive, ancient collision between two collections of galaxies. In it, intracluster gas (represented in pink) and dark matter (represented in blue) have separated.

NASA

[Stacy McGaugh (opens a new tab)](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/), an astronomer at Case Western Reserve University and a longtime proponent of modified-gravity theories, is more skeptical. “It’s not clear to me what the formation mechanism is,” he said. An ancient collision “is a plausible origin story, albeit an exceptional one. If that’s what’s happened, then the rest follows.” In other words: If these galaxies were created when their dark matter was stolen away, then it makes sense that dark matter is a physical substance.

“But the question is: Is that what happened?” he continued. “And I’m not convinced that that’s the only way that can happen.” Without definitively knowing their origin story, McGaugh doesn’t think it’s possible to say anything about the nature of dark matter itself.

Most experts, though, cannot see how DF2, DF4, and DF9 could exist without dark matter being a physical thing, even if the trio’s genesis can be debated. “It’s hard to explain how you’d get something like this evolving by itself without something like dark matter,” Ghag said.

That makes this galactic trio bad news for MOND, or modified Newtonian dynamics, an alternative to dark matter proposed in 1983 by the physicist [Mordehai Milgrom (opens a new tab)](https://weizmann.elsevierpure.com/en/persons/mordehai-milgrom/). “MOND says: What if there’s only visible matter, but its gravity works differently than we thought?” Whiteson explained.

MOND implies that, when objects are experiencing a very weak gravitational pull — for example, when two stars are separated by extreme distances — the gravitational force doesn’t dwindle as much as scientists think. That could explain why spinning galaxies can be held together without needing an extra source of gravity from dark matter, its proponents have argued.

Dark matter has long been the [favored theory (opens a new tab)](https://physicsworld.com/a/mond-versus-dark-matter-the-clash-for-cosmologys-soul/) for cosmologists, as MOND “could never really explain everything,” Ghag said. He explained that MOND suffered a [significant blow (opens a new tab)](https://www.ligo.caltech.edu/news/ligo20160211) in 2015 when the U.S.-based Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, or LIGO, detected gravitational waves — ripples in the fabric of the universe — for the first time. Scientists found that these waves move at the speed of light in all directions over huge distances, which implies that gravity works in a consistent, unmodified way throughout the cosmos.

DF2, DF4, and DF9 are also more elegantly explained by dark matter than by attempts to adjust the mechanics of gravity. “It’s easier to remove matter, cold dark matter, through something like a collision, than it is to turn off a law of nature,” Balaji said.

“I think it’s fine and healthy to have alternative theories and open debate,” Whiteson said. “But let’s also be frank about whether the theory fits the data. MOND does not.”

The identity of dark matter still eludes us. But these galaxies are arguably another nail in the coffin of its increasingly unpopular competitor.

title: NostradamusGPT: The Psychology of Prophecy and How to Break Free from the Prison of Predictive Technologies
content:
[![Image 1: NostradamusGPT: The Psychology of Prophecy and How to Break Free from the Prison of Predictive Technologies](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/veliz_prophecy.jpg?fit=320%2C486&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Prophecy-Prediction-Future-Ancient-Oracles/dp/0385550979/?tag=braipick-20)

This is our paradox: We know that uncertainty is [the substrate of the universe](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/08/20/weeds-and-stars-lisa-rosenberg/), is [the crucible of creativity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/03/27/wislawa-szymborska-nobel-speech/), is [the path to truth](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/10/09/jeff-foster-indecision/), and yet we spend our lives searching for certainty. The word _auspicious_ derives from the Latin _auspex_ — one who examines the flight of birds for omens and [divinations](https://almanacofbirds.org/) of the future. Today, our birds are made of bits — wind-up larks of our own making we call algorithms — but they serve the same function: to let us believe that we can divine the future in order to respond to it; to sedate our anxieties of living by selling us the illusion of control over the unknowable.

All power structures are [prisons we choose to live inside](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/11/11/doris-lessing-massey-lectures/) and all prediction technologies are power structures. Prophets have always been the true governors of empires, first counsels to kings, final ventriloquists of the future.

We can never break free from the uncertainties of living, for we ourselves are [bright violations of probability](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/04/30/bet/), but we can break free from the prison of prediction in order to be more alive: The great mercy of life is that we can change, we can reroute, we can surprise ourselves — that our future is not the computational sum of our past and our destiny not a deterministic equation but an ongoing process constantly creating itself, the way a memory reconstitutes itself with each retelling. Every algorithm that tries to tell us what we will like or do next based on what we have liked or done previously is stealing our self-respect — the respect for the fundamental capacity for self-surprise that makes life worth living — and selling it back to us at the price of the product.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/RedFootedFalcon_lost.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/almanac-of-birds/)

Card from _[An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days](https://www.themarginalian.org/almanac-of-birds/)_, also available as a [stand-alone print](https://www.society6.com/a/products/red-footed-falcon-divination-from-an-almanac-of-birds-divinations-for-uncertain-days8965307_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://www.society6.com/a/products/red-footed-falcon-divination-from-an-almanac-of-birds-divinations-for-uncertain-days8965307_cards?curator=brainpicker).

How to defend this vital aspect of our humanity, of life itself, from the merchants of prediction is what Carissa Véliz explores in [**_Prophecy: Prediction, Power, and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI_**](https://www.amazon.com/Prophecy-Prediction-Future-Ancient-Oracles/dp/0385550979/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/1574786586)) — a book that, in an epoch when it is difficult to say anything original about AI, offers a revelatory look at the prison we have chosen to live inside and a key out.

She writes:

> The computer scientists of today play the same role in power and prophecy as the oracles of the ancient world, the astrologers of the Middle Ages, and the social scientists of the nineteenth century, as we will see… Prophets are merchants of prediction… Artificial intelligence is the new Oracle of Delphi. The likes of Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and Eric Schmidt sharing drinks with presidents and prime ministers is reminiscent of Nostradamus advising Catherine de’ Medici, and Rasputin counseling Nicholas II.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Predictions are often power moves disguised as quests for knowledge. Even when predictions are sincere, they can create currents of political influence that change the world. They become power moves.

She offers a fascinating history of how such technologies of power became possible, became desirable, became the norm — a history that chronicles the shift from the spiritual to the statistical, from faith to blind trust:

> With God gradually moving into a background position, the grip of fate loosened. Along with worldviews that could make sense of and contemplate the notion that chance might play an important role in the world, the invention of printing with movable type in the middle of the fifteenth century facilitated the development of abstract numerical thinking, and with it, scientific inquiry and bureaucratic organization.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Trust in numbers was partly born out of distrust in people.
> 
> 
> It was not only the Church’s disapproval that led to a decline in traditional forms of divination; common people were tired of depending on experts to catch a glimpse of the future. Reading animal entrails or the flight of birds is not obvious, and astrology is technical. The opaqueness of these methods facilitated fabrication, errors, and corruption. Divinatory lots such as dice are ways of potentially communicating with the gods in an open way, visible and readable to all. They also invite asking questions about randomness and probability, which might have contributed to probabilistic thinking. But dice were unfit for purpose in the Enlightenment and beyond. Games of chance were associated with gambling and vice, and leaving decisions to pure chance was counter to rationality. Statistics came to the rescue.
> 
> 
> After getting a kick start from astronomers, statistics developed mostly thanks to bureaucrats who were responding to challenges in public life. It was a practical endeavor, not a scientific one. Merchants, bankers, farmers, militaries, and tax officials needed to count in standardized ways. Extensive trade needs prices and measures, and therefore extensive quantification. As bureaucracies grew, standardization and public justification were necessary. There was also the question of how to hide power struggles to make them look as rational as possible. Numbers, standards, and statistics make politics and power invisible. That’s convenient to anyone wanting to justify what they do as free from values.
> 
> 
> Behind our trust in numbers is a closely related philosophical idea: that values cannot be derived from facts.

Which, of course, they cannot. None of the things we most value — not mountains, not music, not love — can be reduced to a set a facts. Numbers and figures can contour for us what the world is — truly or falsely — but they can never shade in how to live in it, how to share it, how to reshape it into the kind of world we want to live in. Statistical probability will never tell us anything about the reach of possibility. Probability theory pioneer Marc Kac himself [recognized](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/04/mark-kac-enigmas-of-chance-geniuses/) that all creative acts — those triumphs of our humanity — spring from “a world with its own passions, elations and despairs, and it is here that… one may even hear the voice of God.”

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/blake_urizen3.jpg?resize=680%2C490&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/art-by-william-blake-from-the-book-of-urizen-1796_print?curator=brainpicker)

Art from _The First Book of Urizen_ by [William Blake](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/06/18/william-blake-vs-the-world/), 1796. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/art-by-william-blake-from-the-book-of-urizen-1796_print?curator=brainpicker).)

Véliz counters the cultural myth we have been sold:

> The world is not inherently statistical; we made it so by quantifying it, the better to control it.
> 
> 
> Statistics invented society. Since the statistical regularities in phenomena like crime and suicide could not be traced to individual actions, these patterns became attributed to “society” itself. Society became a living entity, above and beyond the individuals constituting it. From 1830, these numerical regularities were interpreted as the most compelling evidence of society’s existence. Statistics invented normal people too.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Probabilistic thinking changed our views of reality (our metaphysics), how we think about what we know (our epistemology), what we count as a good argument and an explanation (our logics), and how we think of the good life (our ethics). It might have even changed the way we think about how we think.

It didn’t just change us, it killed something essential of our nature — the shimmering irregularity that makes each of us who we are, a singular constellation of atoms and story unmatched in all the history and future of the universe. She writes:

> The murderers were philosophers, gamblers, mathematicians, sociologists, insurers, and, above all, bureaucrats. The murder weapons were quantification, data collection, and statistical tools like the normal curve… The motive was power, understood broadly: from astronomers wanting to predict the skies for the purposes of navigation and timekeeping, to insurers wanting to make a profit, to bureaucrats vying for authority and wanting to have more control over the population. We killed individuals with names, personalities, and idiosyncrasies. We killed valuing people for who they are, without attaching categories, numbers, or, worse, rankings to them. We killed our confidence in free will, a topic to which we will come back in chapter eight. We killed trust in people and replaced it with trust in numbers. We gained order, but it came at a price. What we lost is rarely subject to quantification. But that it cannot be quantified doesn’t mean that it didn’t exist or matter.

In a passage that calls to mind Ursula K. Le Guin’s eternal insistence that [“words are events, they do things, change things,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/22/telling-is-listening-ursula-k-le-guin-communication/) she adds:

> We do things with words, other than describe the world. Predictions are not mere assertions; they are acts in the world, and that is a further reason why they are not facts. Predictions are speech acts: assertions that do something.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> When someone makes a prediction, depending on the context and their methods, as well as their will to power (what they want), they might be doing very different things: expressing their degree of confidence about something, expressing the chances of something happening in the world, expressing what they want the world to look like in the future, trying to manipulate their audience into buying what they sell, or a combination… What they are not doing, however, is uttering a true statement about the world.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Predictive societies tend toward oppression through surveillance and self-fulfilling prophecies because predictions are speech acts that are closer to commands than to truth claims.

(Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/art-from-thomas-wrights-an-original-theory-or-new-hypothesis-of-the-universe-17504457506_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://society6.com/brainpicker/collection/vintage-science-cards?curator=brainpicker).)

Given [our cognitive apparatus is wired for our expectations to shape our reality](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/06/20/the-experience-machine-andy-clark/), the predictions we believe end up shaping our lives:

> A prediction about people has reflexive qualities, acting like a magnet that bends reality toward itself. When the force of the magnet is strong enough, the prediction becomes the cause of its becoming true.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Predictions are commands disguised as descriptions… Predictions change the reality they purport to predict, and sometimes their accuracy is evidence not of knowledge or understanding but of despotism.

Our greatest frontier of resistance is to remember that we can be the makers of our own destiny with our choices, but our choices are driven by our beliefs, which are the easiest thing to manipulate and imprison in a power structure, and therefore the first thing that must break free. Véliz — who delves deeper into these questions in this [excellent _Where Shall We Meet_ interview](https://www.whereshallwemeet.xyz/2372295/episodes/19830715-on-prophecy-with-carissa-veliz) — insists that the key is in our hands if we keep in mind — our gloriously fractal, wildly associative, defiantly illogical mind — a few truths about being human that the prophets of prediction try to obscure:

> *   What we deem inevitable often never comes to pass, while what we thought impossible awaits around the corner.
> *   Spaces of indeterminacy are where creativity, humor, and innovation flourish.
> *   Allowing defiance is the right way to treat human beings, who are ends in themselves, with their own idiosyncratic views and preferences. Every life is worth living, every life a work of art to be created much more than discovered.
> *   We shape our ideas and our ideas shape us

Reflecting on the tapestry of paradoxes threading through our yearning for control and our vulnerability to exploitation, she asks:

> Unpredictability, arising from partial knowledge, social complexity and reflexivity, scientific and technological breakthroughs, flukes, and blindness, is never going away. Given this unsettling fact of life, how should we live?

The best answer I know is [this Marie Howe poem](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/05/16/marie-howe-the-maples/).
